opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's one of the most interesting open problems right now. I like to think about it in terms of the human brain. System one is fast, intuitive, almost reflexive: the motor control that lets you catch a ball or keep your balance without thinking about it. System two is slow and deliberate: planning, reasoning, deciding what to do next. "I need to go to the kitchen, open the fridge, grab the milk."

For robots, these two systems have very different requirements. The low-level motor control has to run at a very high frequency, hundreds of hertz or even a thousand, so the robot can react to contact and disturbances in real time. Reasoning and planning can run much slower, maybe once a second or a few times a second, but it needs a lot more world knowledge and semantic understanding. That's where vision-language models come in, because they've absorbed so much common sense from internet-scale data.

So the challenge is how you connect the two. One approach is a hierarchical design: a big vision-language model as the slow thinker that produces plans or intermediate representations, and a smaller, faster policy that turns those into motor actions. That's roughly the philosophy we took with GR00T N1, a dual-system architecture where the system two module interprets the scene and the instruction, and the system one module generates fluid actions in real time.

The tricky part is the interface. What exactly gets passed from system two to system one? If it's natural language, it may be too coarse. "Pick up the cup" doesn't tell you how to grasp it. If it's something more latent, like embeddings, you get more expressiveness but lose interpretability, and it's harder to train. And you want the whole thing trained end to end, so the reasoning knows what the motor system can actually do, and the motor system can take advantage of the reasoning.

Then there's the data question, which I always come back to. System two can lean on internet data, but system one needs physical interaction data, which is scarce. So we use a data pyramid: internet video and web data at the base, lots of simulation and synthetic data in the middle, and a thin but very precious layer of real-robot teleoperation data at the top. Getting both systems to benefit from all of it is a big part of the puzzle.

Long term, I think the line between the two may blur, much like in humans. We don't really have two separate brains. It's one neural system with different modes. Eventually I'd love to see a single model that adaptively decides how much to think before it acts. For now, though, the dual-system design is a very practical way to get the best of both worlds.

r001.rationale: The candidate calls integration an open problem and contrasts a current dual-system design with a hoped-for future single model. It does not clearly frame choosing between those architectures as an open architectural question.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is really the central question for me right now. The way I think about it is that a robot foundation model has to do two very different jobs at the same time, and those jobs run at completely different clocks.

System one is the fast, reactive, almost reflexive part. When you reach out and grab a coffee cup, you're not thinking about the trajectory of your wrist. That loop has to run at something like a hundred, two hundred hertz on a humanoid, because if you're even a little bit late, the robot falls over or crushes the cup. System two is the slow, deliberate part. That's where you read the scene, understand the task, break it down into steps, notice that the cup is actually behind a jar and you need to move the jar first. That's a vision-language model territory, and those things run at maybe a few hertz at best, and that's being generous.

So the naive approach is to just bolt a big VLM on top of a motor controller and have them talk. And that works for demos, but what you find is the handoff is where everything breaks. The language model says "pick up the red block," and the low-level policy doesn't really have a grounded notion of what the language model meant. They've been trained separately, they don't share a representation, and so the errors compound at the interface.

What we did with GR00T was try to make that a single end-to-end model, but with two components that are co-trained. The system two module is a VLM that looks at the images and the instruction and produces a kind of latent plan, a representation that encodes "here's what I'm trying to do right now." And then the system one module is a diffusion transformer that takes that latent and outputs a chunk of motor actions, continuous joint targets, at high frequency. The important part is that the gradient flows across the boundary. So the slow part learns to produce latents that the fast part can actually use, and the fast part learns to interpret those latents in a way that's grounded in the actual physics of the body.

The hard engineering problem is the asynchrony. You can't wait for the VLM every time you want to emit an action. So the fast module has to be able to act on a slightly stale plan, and the slow module has to update that plan in the background. It's a bit like how a human driver works: your attention is updated maybe a few times a second, but your hands are making micro-corrections constantly, using the last thing your attention told them.

And then there's the data question, which I think is actually where most of the difficulty lives. The system two part benefits enormously from internet-scale data, videos of humans, text, all of that. The system one part needs real embodied data, teleoperation, simulation, and that's scarce. So you end up with this data pyramid where you have a huge base of web data, a middle layer of synthetic and simulation data, and a tiny tip of real robot data, and the architecture has to be designed so each layer actually teaches the right module. If you're not careful, the real robot data gets drowned out and the model learns to talk about tasks instead of doing them.

The thing I'm genuinely uncertain about is whether this two-module split is a permanent architectural feature or a temporary scaffold. In language models, we didn't engineer a separate "reasoning module," the chain of thought kind of emerged from scale. So it's possible that with enough embodied data, a single model learns to internally allocate compute between fast and slow. But I don't think we're there yet, and in the meantime, making the division explicit is the thing that actually works on a real robot.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly questions whether the two-module split is permanent or a temporary scaffold, and considers whether a single model could learn to allocate compute between fast and slow reasoning.

astra-6.text:
I think the key challenge is that these two systems operate at very different timescales. System two might reason about a task, break it into steps, and decide what to do next. But system one has to keep the robot moving and responding to the world while that reasoning is happening. You can’t stop balancing or controlling your hand every time you need to think.

So the interface between them is really important. What does the reasoning system send to the motor system? Is it language, a goal state, or some learned representation? And what does the motor system send back when something unexpected happens? If you’re trying to pick up a cup and it slips, you need an immediate correction. You don’t want to wait for a long reasoning process.

I think we need a tight feedback loop, where reasoning guides action and action continuously grounds the reasoning. The hard part is making that work reliably, with the right amount of thinking at the right moment.

r001.rationale: The response discusses how system two reasoning and system one motor control should communicate, but it does not frame a choice between one monolithic model and separate models as an open architectural question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is that they operate at very different timescales. System two might reason about a task: what the goal is, what steps are needed, and what to do if something goes wrong. System one has to turn that plan into motion, reacting continuously to what the robot sees and feels. You don’t want the robot deliberating over every tiny adjustment of its fingers.

The hard part is the interface between them. A high-level plan can sound perfectly reasonable and still be physically impossible. So system two needs to be grounded in what the robot can actually do, and system one needs a way to signal uncertainty or failure back up. It has to be a closed loop.

For example, if you ask a robot to pick up a cup, the reasoning system might decide where to grasp it. But as the hand makes contact, the motor system needs to adapt immediately. If the cup slips or turns out to be too heavy, that feedback may require a new plan.

So I’d think of it as a hierarchy with continuous feedback. The goal is to let deliberate reasoning guide fast, learned behavior without becoming a bottleneck for every action.

r001.rationale: The response describes a hierarchy with feedback between system two and system one, but does not present the choice between one monolithic model and separate communicating models as an open architectural question.
